questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I decided to go on exchange because I was really attracted to the idea of studying abroad. I wanted to gain a broader, more international perspective on law, which I think is essential for today’s lawyers. Additionally, having traveled solo in the past, I’ve experienced firsthand how much personal growth comes from stepping outside your comfort zone. I knew this exchange would be an opportunity for both professional and personal development.

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Finding accommodation can be quite challenging, especially with so many international students competing for the same places. However, with some effort and persistence, it’s definitely possible. Everyone I met, including myself, managed to secure housing in the end.

First and foremost, accommodation in San Diego is expensive—particularly if you want to live near popular areas like Mission Beach or Pacific Beach, where many international students choose to stay. I lived in an apartment with five other Danes. The apartment had three bedrooms, so each of us shared a room with another student. Sharing a room is very common among students, as having a private room is often too costly.

We found our apartment on Airbnb and negotiated a better price with the owner since we were staying long term. Others I know contacted local real estate agents, but reaching out to them can be easier once you're already in San Diego. My advice is to start looking for accommodation as early as possible to increase your chances of finding something suitable.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
Getting accepted to USD involves meeting several requirements.

First, you need to pass the TOEFL test with a minimum score of 93, which can be challenging. Second, you must provide at least one recommendation letter from an academic who is familiar with your legal skills and qualifications. Third, you’ll need to secure health insurance that meets USD’s strict requirements. This can be difficult, but after trying several options, we eventually found suitable coverage through Gouda. Finally, you must demonstrate sufficient financial resources, which requires proof of at least 120,000 DKK.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: It was possible to ask questions to USD regarding what the different requirements included.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
It was very successful—I managed to get almost all the courses I wanted.

Once you’re accepted at USD, they invite you to an individual orientation session that explains how to search for and apply for courses. During this meeting, they also provide guidance on the number of credits you need and recommend courses that are well-suited for international exchange students.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Start good time in advance on preparing your documents for the application. Talk with other students who are in the same situation as you. Speak with former students if you know any.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I highly recommend all of these courses.

Intro to US Law is mandatory, but I thoroughly enjoyed the other four courses as well. My schedule only required me to attend classes two days a week, and many of the courses didn’t have a traditional final exam. Instead, grades were based on assignments and submissions throughout the semester.

Negotiation was a fantastic and enjoyable class. The professor was incredibly kind, approachable, and showed a genuine interest in the international students. Each class involved preparing for roleplays, where you were paired with a random classmate. This was a great way to connect with American students and improve your English skills in a fun, interactive setting.

Corporate Innovation had a higher academic and legal level compared to the other courses, with higher expectations for students. However, it was incredibly engaging and focused on how AI is impacting the legal profession and innovation. The exam consisted of writing a paper and presenting it to the class. Although the assignment was challenging, I learned a great deal from this course and highly recommend it for those interested in the intersection of law and technology.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I enjoyed surfing. San Diego is a hot spot for surfing, so if you’re even slightly interested, it’s definitely worth giving it a try. The city also offers many social clubs, often centered around sports or outdoor activities. Joining one of these clubs is a great way to meet locals and connect with others who share your interests. You can easily find these social clubs on Instagram.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Spend days in the beach. Go to La Jolla and watch the sealions. Visit Downtown San Diego, Old Town and Little Italy. Visit Navy Seals Museum. Spend a day surfing. Walk around in Pacific Beach area.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I found it very easy. Americans are incredibly open-minded, making it feel natural and effortless to strike up a conversation with a stranger.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Go up and talk to people on the beach or at bars. Participate in the social clubs mentioned above.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The beautiful nature and the americans openminded attitude. It really spreads positive energy.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) prepare your administrative documents good time in advance. Make deadlines for your self, so you don't loose track of important deadlines. 
2) Go on roadtrip and explore as much of california as possible. 
3) Get out of your comfortzoen and try to engage with Americans (and not only Danes or other scandinavian exchange students). By embracing their culture of being open minded and non-judging,  you can make so many good relations and have interesting conversations.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Take the time to thoroughly review all the specific requirements for applying to USD. Create a detailed timeline with deadlines, and schedule important appointments with your teacher, bank, U.S. embassy, TOEFL test center, and any other necessary institutions. Acting early is crucial, as the process is lengthy and involves significant administrative work. Being proactive will help you stay on track and reduce stress as you navigate the application process.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Living in San Diego and being part of it's laid-back, sunny, surfing culture. People are so happy, active and genuine.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Being on my own, far from everyone and everything familiar, was a challenge. Stepping out of your comfort zone will inevitably feel strange and uncomfortable at times, but that’s only because we do it so rarely. Try to embrace the experience—being on your own can be incredibly rewarding. Once you’ve done it a few times, you’ll realize it’s not as intimidating as it seems. In fact, it can be an opportunity for growth and self-discovery.
